ch25.title: Pentecost
ch25.b002: Andrew was counting heads. The upper chamber of Mary Mark’s house was the room where thirteen men had usually sat to break bread, but by half past ten that morning people filled it to the landing of the stair and crowded the window ledges. At Peter’s word, John Mark and some others had spent the morning going through the city calling them in, the foremost of the Master’s disciples living in Jerusalem. One hundred. One hundred and ten. One hundred and twenty. Andrew set the figure down in his mind and went on from face to face. Among them was Mary, the mother of the Master. She sat quietly beside John, her face aged but composed. James, the Master’s brother, was there too, leaning against the wall. Only a few years earlier he had kept his distance, unable to understand his eldest brother.
ch25.b003: Counting was an old habit of Andrew’s. Who had come, who was missing, who was worn out. He was chief of the apostolic corps, and the chief was always the one who checked last. Yet this morning his reckoning kept slipping. Even as his finger moved from person to person, another scene laid itself over the room. The western slope of the Mount of Olives, two thirds of the way up. Half past seven in the morning, the walls of Jerusalem spread out below and the olive trees of Gethsemane crouching dark green beneath them. From the moment they left the upper chamber no one had said a single word. And when the Master halted and turned to face them, without anyone telling them to, they had knelt around him.
ch25.b004: In a circle. In that moment Andrew had known what his knees were remembering. The winter grass on the highland north of Capernaum, the chill of the ground coming up through the cloth of his robe. That day the Master’s hands had passed over the heads of the twelve one by one and had come to rest, last of all, on his. This morning the Master had stood before them as they knelt and told them again to stay in the city until they were clothed with power from on high. He had told them to love men as he had loved them and serve men as he had served them. And then he had bidden them farewell. At about a quarter to eight he vanished from before their eyes. For a long time afterward Andrew could not unbend his knees. The place above his head was empty.
ch25.b005: At the front of the room Peter rose. He said he would speak for his fellow apostles, and no one stopped him. Since their return from Galilee Peter had simply come to stand in that place. The Master had never given him such authority, and the apostles had never chosen him; but he was the best speaker among them, and so they all took it as a matter of course. Peter told of the last morning on the mountain: the kneeling circle, the final charge, the disappearance. His voice wavered a few times and rose a few times. The people held their breath. Somewhere among the women someone was weeping without a sound. It took him not quite an hour, and Andrew watched the story plant a new memory of that morning on the mountain in every person in the room. Even those who had not been there were kneeling on that slope now.
ch25.b006: Peter himself, as he spoke, did not know where his voice was coming from. He had not said a single word on the hillside that morning, and the silence was still inside him. So he spoke slowly, which was unlike him. Several times he stopped and looked out of the window. The sky into which the Master had gone was no different from any other May sky. He found he did not resent it. The one who was leaving had said he would not leave them alone. He had said he would send something else. Peter did not know what it was, or when it would come. He only knew that this time he would wait. He would not draw a sword, and he would not cast a net.
ch25.b007: Watching his brother’s profile, Andrew remembered something that shamed him. It was the evening of the resurrection day, when Peter had come bursting breathless into this very upper chamber, crying that he had seen the Master in the garden and that the Master had forgiven him. The others had been just on the point of laying their doubts aside, and Andrew had stood up and warned them not to be swept along by his brother’s report. He had hinted that Peter had seen things before that were not there. It had not been a false thing to say. But it had not been a true one either. A few days later, on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, the Master had walked beside Andrew and asked whether he trusted him. And then he had told him that if he did, he must trust his brethren more, even Peter. Since that day Andrew had not let one day pass without turning those words over.
ch25.b009: When Peter had finished his account, he announced that the apostles had decided to choose someone to fill the place of Judas Iscariot. Two men had been put forward, Matthias and Justus. There would be a short pause, he said, while the apostles decided between them. The eleven went down the narrow stair to the room below.
ch25.b010: The lower room was cool. From the direction of the kitchen came a faint smell of wood smoke and boiling barley. The eleven stood in a ring: Peter and Andrew, James and John, Philip and Nathaniel, Matthew and Thomas, James and Judas, the Alpheus twins, and Simon Zelotes. Once they had formed their ring, there was a gap on one side of it. No one looked at that place. Everyone knew it. The head on which the Master’s hand had first rested on the highland; the back of a man sitting alone under a fig tree, gazing at the eastern sky. That was what belonged there.
ch25.b011: “Let’s not choose by our own judgment. Let’s cast lots.”
ch25.b012: Someone said it, and they all nodded. There was not much discussion. Not one of the eleven had the confidence to choose between the two. Choosing a man was something that had already wounded them deeply once.
ch25.b013: Andrew listened to the rattle of the lots and looked down at his own palm. He had known before anyone. While the others suspected nothing, he had noticed that Judas’s laugh came a fraction late, that his words of agreement ended a little too short. And he had said nothing. To speak aloud of something he was not sure of was not his way. Whether that way had been right, he still did not know. But now he knew something else. What he had left unsaid in those days was not only his suspicion of Judas. He had never once given Judas a kind word either. He had not gone over to him when he sat alone under the fig tree. Praise, comfort, warning: none of it had ever got past his throat. If an isolated man breaks, does the silence of those who left him isolated weigh nothing at all? Andrew did not turn away from the thought. In the upper chamber, before they climbed the mountain, the Master had said that Judas was gone because his love had grown cold and he had refused to trust his brethren, and that they must therefore trust each other and confide in each other. To Andrew those words sounded like words about himself before they were words about Judas.
ch25.b014: Peter too was trying not to look at the empty place. When he heard how Judas had ended, he had shuddered. And what tormented him most in the days afterward was not grief but a question. What makes me any different? Judas took silver and handed the Master over; Peter, before a serving girl’s teasing, had said he did not know him. Both of them had forsaken him. After that night Peter had wrestled a long time with the thought that he, too, was a betrayer. It was not his own resolve that ended that struggle. It was the one who came to find him in the garden. Had there been no such garden for Judas? There had. The Master had left the door open to him to the very end. Only Judas never once turned toward it. He did not open his heart to his brethren, and he never went to the Master with a trouble of his own. Peter thought he was beginning to see a little of what had been different in himself. Whenever he wavered, he had poured it all out to his brother. Whenever he fell, he had wept aloud. That was what had saved him.
ch25.b015: The lot fell on Matthias. For a moment Matthias stood there dazed, and then he bowed his head. He was received as an apostle on the spot and then named treasurer. Someone handed him the money purse. The eleven watched it pass from hand to hand without a word. The leather strap had been worn smooth and shiny. Matthew quietly lowered his eyes. Of everyone in that room, only Matthew knew who had secretly refilled that purse each time it ran low.
ch25.b016: It was close to noon when they went back upstairs and announced that Matthias had been chosen. Then Peter asked everyone to join in prayer, that they might be made ready for the gift of the spirit the Master had promised he would send.
ch25.b018: The room grew still. One hundred and twenty people bowed their heads where they sat. Some knelt; some leaned their backs against the wall. The May light from the window lay slantwise across the floor. Outside, the city was loud with the festival. In every lane the footsteps of pilgrims and the sounds of many languages ran together. The noise came in at the open window and died away as it met the silence of the room.
ch25.b019: Peter sat with his eyes closed. He did not know what to ask for. When it came to praying he had always had a great deal to say, but over these forty days his prayers had grown shorter and shorter. Whatever he had needed to be forgiven, he had been forgiven. As for a second chance, he had been given that three times over on the beach. What remained was waiting. He did not know how to wait. All his life he had moved before he thought and spoken before he resolved. And now here he sat doing nothing. He had nothing to say and no net to cast. The emptiness of his hands was strange to him, and the strangeness was oddly peaceful.
ch25.b020: It was about one o’clock. Something was in the room.
ch25.b021: No wind had blown, and no light had flashed. The door stood as it had stood, and the light by the window lay just where it had lain a moment before. Only, all at once, the hundred and twenty knew that someone had come into the room. Peter opened his eyes. He saw no one. And yet he was not alone. Something welled up from deep in his chest. It was joy, but not the joy he knew. It was not giddy, and it did not waver. It was a joy that stood with its feet firm on the ground. A sense of being safe, a certainty that whatever came now would be well, wrapped that joy around. All at once he could not tell where the fear had gone that had clung to his back for forty days. He looked for it, and it was not there.
ch25.b022: Across the room Andrew felt the same thing. Out of habit he looked round at the faces. John’s face was wet. Thomas had lifted his head as if to measure something, and then, at length, he closed his eyes. The twins were looking at each other and smiling without a sound. Simon Zelotes unclenched his fists and laid his open palms upon his knees. The Master’s mother sat with her hands folded and did not move, and the women around her were the same. This had not come to the apostles alone. It had come just the same to the women, to the disciples whose names no one would remember, to the Master’s own family. It had come to no one more and to no one less. Andrew saw that. And he stopped counting. There was no need to count. No one had been left out.
ch25.b023: Philip sat on the floor looking down at his two hands. All his life he had been the man who asked to be shown. Now he could see nothing at all, and yet he asked nothing more. Nathaniel thought of no jest, just as on the day of their ordination on the highland. Matthias, the newest apostle, looked about him at first like a man who had no idea what was happening, and then he too grew still like the rest. He had become an apostle that morning, and an hour later he had received exactly what all of them received. There was no difference there between those who had come first and those who came last.
ch25.b024: Close behind that quiet joy came something else. They wanted to go out. They wanted to leave this room and go into the streets, among the people, and speak: the good news of the kingdom, and that the Master had risen from the dead. In Peter that urge became a deed first. He rose to his feet.
ch25.b025: Peter said that this could only be the Spirit of Truth, come as the Master had promised. And he proposed that they go to the temple and begin there to proclaim the good news that had been put into their hands. No one objected. Not even Thomas objected. They did just as Peter said.
ch25.b027: The moment he came down the stair and stepped out of the Marks’ door, the sunlight dazzled Peter. Forty days. For forty days they had been in hiding. Apart from the time in Galilee, he had hardly once walked a main street of this city by daylight. The door had always been barred, the shutters always half closed, and a single footstep on the stair had made everyone hold his breath. And now he was walking down the middle of the road. Pilgrims jostled past, shoulder to shoulder. It was Pentecost. Thousands who had come from every part of the world filled the city, and many had stayed on ever since the Passover. The Passover. At that word Peter’s step grew heavy for a moment.
ch25.b028: That night had happened in the courtyard of Annas, on the slope of Mount Olivet. It was a chilly night, and a charcoal fire burned in the middle of the court. He had pushed in among the high priest’s servants to warm his hands. The girl who kept the gate had asked him, half in mischief, whether he was not one of that man’s disciples too. Faced with a sword’s point, he would not have given way. He had in fact drawn his sword in the garden. But before that one mocking question he had shriveled. I am not. The words came out before he could think, and once out, they dragged the next words after them, and the next. When the cock crowed, the doors opened, and the Master, being led away, looked at him. There was no reproach in that look. That was what broke him.
ch25.b029: More than three years before that, he had stood by another fire. On the night of the ordination, in Zebedee’s garden, the twins had built a small fire. In its light he had spoken for all of them: not one of them would turn back; they would drink the cup. There had not been a grain of falsehood in it. And he had not kept it. For a long time afterward Peter had measured the distance between those two fires. How had he come from that fire to this one? On the night he sat by the roadside weeping, he had gone looking for his brother. Andrew was in hiding, and David Zebedee sent a messenger to show Peter where. Andrew asked him nothing. Not then, and not afterward. And when the time came, he led him back to the nets and set his hands working again. That wordless understanding was what had held him.
ch25.b030: And then there was the garden. On the evening of the resurrection day the Master had come to find him in the garden of the Mark home. They had talked only a few minutes, but those few minutes paid for three days of nights. And then there was the shore of the Sea of Galilee. Do you love me? Three questions, three answers. At the third he had been a little hurt, as though the Master did not trust him. But now he understood. The mouth that had denied him again and again was being made to say again and again that it loved him. Feed my sheep. And follow me to the end.
ch25.b032: Peter glanced sideways as he walked. Andrew was there. Half a step behind, as always.
ch25.b035: Andrew asked nothing more. The two of them climbed the steps toward the temple.
ch25.b036: Andrew walked with his eyes on his brother’s back. He could guess what Peter had started to say and then let go. Most likely he too was thinking of that night. Under these same walls, on the other side of this same city, Peter had wandered looking for him. All Andrew could do then was to ask nothing. Today, too, he asked nothing. But today’s silence was not the silence of that night. Then he had kept quiet because he did not know what to say. Today he kept quiet because nothing needed to be said. His brother’s stride did not falter.
ch25.b038: At about two o’clock Peter stood up in a certain spot in the temple court. It was the very place where the Master had last taught in the temple. No one had chosen it. His feet had simply taken him there. Six apostles took part in that gathering: Peter, Andrew, James, John, Philip, and Matthew. Where the others were at that hour Andrew failed to notice that day. Once again he had forgotten to count. Twice in one day.
ch25.b039: Peter began to speak. At his first few words people merely slowed their pace. At festival time there was always someone in the temple courts shouting about something. But soon they stopped, and others gathered behind those who had stopped, and still more behind them. Peter spoke of Jesus of Nazareth, a man whom God had made known by works of great power and by wonders. He had been handed over, Peter said, according to God’s settled purpose and foreknowledge, and these very people had crucified him and put him to death. What God had told beforehand through the mouths of the prophets had been fulfilled in this way. But God had raised him up again. God had made him both Lord and Christ.
ch25.b040: Peter did not fully know what he was saying. The words were there before he chose them. Yet they were not like the words of the old days, leaping out ahead of his thoughts. Something beside him was handing him the words. He did not stop to ask what it was. Only, there was one strange thing. He was not aware of the presence that had come into the room. What he was aware of was the Master. It was as if the Master were standing just behind him, somewhere in the shade of the temple columns, watching him. Peter looked at the crowd. Among those faces might be someone who had shouted for crucifixion outside Pilate’s headquarters that Friday morning. Someone might be a servant who had pointed his finger at him in the courtyard of Annas. He was not afraid of them. He was not rebuking them. He was calling them. As the Master had once called him.
ch25.b041: Andrew watched his brother. It was a voice he knew. It was the voice that had haggled over wages with a dealer at the fish-drying sheds of Bethsaida when they were young, the voice that had shouted against the wind out on the middle of the lake. But within that voice was something that had never been there before. It did not hurry. The words did not outrun the thoughts. Words and thoughts walked in step. Peter said that this Jesus, lifted up to the right hand of God and having received from the Father the promised spirit, had poured out what they now saw and heard. So they must repent, he said, so that their sins might be wiped away and the Father might send them the Christ appointed for them.
ch25.b042: The apostles spoke in Greek, in Hebrew, in Aramaic. When they noticed people in the crowd who spoke another tongue, they offered them a few words in their own language, whatever bits each of them had picked up. Galilee was a crossroads where people of many nations came and went. John never left Peter’s right side. For more than an hour and a half the speaking did not stop.
ch25.b043: Andrew watched the faces in the crowd. That was his work. He was no preacher. But of all the twelve, he had the sharpest eye for men. He saw that among the people standing in the shade of the temple columns were some who wore the dress of the high priest’s household. Astonishment rose in their faces, and then, after one look around at the crowd, it turned into something else. Fear. They were calculating that if they laid a hand on these men now, this crowd would not stand by. Andrew read the calculation. Then he looked at his brother again. Peter did not so much as glance their way. The man who forty days ago had shriveled at a serving girl’s single word was now standing before that girl’s masters and not turning his back.
ch25.b044: Andrew remembered the day on the highland. As they sat around him, the Master had told them that some of them would not die until they had seen the reign of God come in great power. That day Peter’s eyes had shone and Simon Zelotes had clenched his fist. Both of them had been thinking of swords and thrones. Over the next four years those words had been turned over among them many times. But now, in the temple court, Andrew felt that he was beginning, for the first time, to make out a little of what they meant. The power had come. Without an army and without a throne, in the hoarse voice of a Galilean fisherman. Whether that was all the words meant, he did not know. But that it was part of their meaning, he was sure.
ch25.b045: Looking back long afterward, it would be clear that what they proclaimed that day was somewhat different from the message the Master had entrusted to them. He had told them to preach the love of the Father in heaven and that all men are his children, and he had said that his rising from the dead did not change that message. But on that day the greatest news that filled their hearts was the risen Master himself. So they proclaimed him. Peter led the way and the others followed. What that would one day change, no one in that court knew. Still, many of the truths he had taught were carried along inside their words. And the people who heard those words came to him.
ch25.b047: By half past four the people began to move. There were more than two thousand. The apostles led them down from the temple to the pool of Siloam at the southern end of the city. The narrow lanes filled with people. In all the noise of the festival it was a strangely quiet procession. Andrew looked back as he walked. He could not see the end of it.
ch25.b048: Pentecost was the great festival of baptism. On this day Jews, and gentiles who knocked at the gate wishing to serve Yahweh, went down into the water. So no one thought it strange that thousands should gather at a pool. Peter and Andrew, James and John stepped into the water. The May water was colder than they expected. The four of them baptized the people one by one in the Master’s name.
ch25.b049: Andrew took each one who came to him by the shoulders, laid him back beneath the water, and raised him up again. The next, and the next. These were the hands that had dragged nets. All his life they had gripped wet ropes and slippery fish. And now there were people in those hands. Fishers of men. When the Master first said it, he had heard it as a figure of speech. Today it was no figure. The weight of wet cloth against his palms, the gasp as someone came up out of the water, someone’s chin trembling: he received each of these with his hands. There was an old Greek-speaking merchant, and a boy with a frightened face, and a woman who came up out of the water and would not let go of his hand.
ch25.b050: A few paces away in the water, Peter was doing the same work. Each time he raised someone from the water, he looked into the face. What kind of night had this one come through? Whom had he denied, what had he forsaken? There was no way to know. But he saw on every face that rose from the water the look of someone who had set something down. He knew that look. His own face, standing alone in the garden of the Mark home after the Master had gone, must have looked like that. Only one who has been forgiven can hand forgiveness on. Peter was learning that today. The teaching about forgiving not seven times but seventy times and seven was growing wet and heavy in his palms.
ch25.b051: Matthew stood at the edge of the pool and watched. The four standing in the water were the four fishermen. That seemed right to him. He kept watch over the cloaks and sandals people had left on the stones, and handed dry cloths to those who came shivering out of the water. Someone thanked him. That person did not know he had once sat at the customs house in Capernaum. Today, at this pool, no one asked. For Matthew, that was enough.
ch25.b052: The sun went down. The stones around the pool turned red and then gray. Someone brought torches. By the time the last person came up out of the water it was already dark. The four came up out of the pool trailing their wet robes. Their legs were trembling. John dropped down onto a stone step, and James sat beside him. Nobody said anything.
ch25.b053: John sat on the step with his face against his knees and then lifted his head. All day he had stood at Peter’s side. A few years earlier he would have been a little proud of that place: one of the three closest to the Master, and today at the right hand of the chief preacher. But today the thought had not come to him once. He had simply looked at the four men standing in the water and been glad that he and his brother were among them. Without a word, James brushed the water from his younger brother’s wet hair with the flat of his hand. These were the two who had once been called the sons of thunder.
ch25.b055: The people scattered, and the torches drifted away one by one. James and John were the first to get up, following Philip and Matthew back into the city. Only the two brothers remained by the pool. Andrew squatted at the water’s edge below the stone steps and wrung out his wet cloak. The water ran down over his wrists. Peter sat on a stone a little way off, looking at the dark water. For a man who had poured out words all day long, he was very quiet. His voice was hoarse.
ch25.b056: Andrew looked at his brother’s back. He had been looking at that back his whole life. After their father died, he, the eldest, had kept the household together, and his brother had grown up beside him. Brother and brother had lived that way, each filling up what the other lacked. The younger spoke before he thought; the elder thought longer than he spoke. The younger told everything first to his brother, and the elder, for the most part, listened. And then came that day by the Jordan. After his first walk with the Master, he had gone back to the camp and before anything else had gone to find his brother: this man was the great Teacher, he had said, and Simon too should go to him and offer himself. From then on the younger had overtaken the elder. He became one of the three closest to the Master, and today he had moved the hearts of two thousand people. It did not hurt Andrew. It had never once hurt him. That had always seemed a little strange, even to himself.
ch25.b057: What had hurt was something else. He did not know how to praise. To tell someone that he had done well always seemed too close to flattery. And so all his life he had not said it. On the night of the ordination, by the fire, when his brother had spoken the vow for everyone, he had said nothing; instead he had reached out and laid his hand on his brother’s shoulder, like the hand that had rested on his own head that afternoon. That had been enough, he believed. But he remembered a man sitting alone under a fig tree. He knew now what weight words never spoken could come to carry. And today the quiet joy that had entered the room had loosened something that had long been set hard somewhere in his throat. Trust one another, confide in one another. Trust your brethren more. Even Peter.
ch25.b058: Andrew laid his wet cloak across his knee and stood up. He went over and sat down beside his brother. The smell of water mingled with the smell of torch smoke. For a long while he stayed as he was. Then he spoke.
ch25.b060: Peter turned to look at him.
ch25.b061: “I couldn’t do what you did today. I never will.”
ch25.b062: Andrew stopped there. It was where he always stopped. The next words caught in his throat. He pushed them out.
ch25.b063: “But I’m glad I have a brother who could.”
ch25.b064: Peter could not say anything. He looked at his brother. In the dark he could hardly make out his face. But he knew that voice. It was a voice he had heard all his life, and a voice that had never once in all his life said anything like this. Peter’s lips trembled. All day he had spoken before two thousand people without a stumble. And now, before his one brother, the words would not come.
ch25.b065: At last he spoke. His voice was rough.
ch25.b066: “If it weren’t for you, I wouldn’t have been there today. You’re the one who took me to him. And every time I swung this way and that, you were always right there, the same as ever, and that’s how I managed to stay by his side.”
ch25.b067: Even after that night by the charcoal fire, he almost added, and then didn’t. His brother knew. He too remembered that wordless hand that had led him back to the nets without a single question.
ch25.b068: For a while the two sat without speaking. In the darkness the water of Siloam lapped softly. Then Peter laughed, a laugh that was half a sob.
ch25.b069: “So you can say things like that.”
ch25.b070: As he said it, Peter remembered Zebedee’s garden, the night his brother’s hand had come to rest on his shoulder after he made his vow. That night his brother had said nothing, and Peter had believed that the hand alone told him everything in his brother’s heart. But the words he had heard today were different from that hand. A hand receives. A word gives. For thirty years and more his brother had only received him: every time he fell, every time he wavered, every time he ran on ahead. Today for the first time his brother had given him something. Peter took it with both hands. He thought he would never forget it as long as he lived. This time he made no vow. He knew he would not forget it, vow or no vow.
ch25.b072: Andrew said it, and then he laughed too. He reached out and laid his hand on his brother’s shoulder, as he had in Zebedee’s garden. But this time the word had come before the hand. For the first time in more than thirty years.
ch25.b074: They got up and walked back into the city. The lanes were dark, and festival lamps glowed through the doorways. Somewhere a psalm was being sung. Their wet clothes were heavy, but their feet were light. Andrew walked half a step behind, as always. That was his place, and he did not mind it.
ch25.b075: From tomorrow, people would call his brother Simon Peter. And they would call him Simon Peter’s brother. Andrew knew it. He thought he would not mind being called that for the rest of his life. The first one called would be remembered as the brother of the second. That did not trouble him in the least. Perhaps, from the day by the Jordan when he first went to find his brother and urged him to go to the Master, he had been called to be exactly that kind of man.
ch25.b076: A light was still burning in the upper chamber of the Marks’ house. Laughter and talk came tumbling down the stair. He could hear Thomas’s voice, and the twins laughing, and then Nathaniel said something and everyone laughed at once. The deep voice of Simon Zelotes was mixed in among them. Andrew stopped for a moment at the foot of the stair and listened to those voices. He did not count. There was no need to count.
ch25.b077: From now on they would gather in the temple day after day with one heart, break bread in their homes, and share what they had. And in less than a month they would grow more in spirit than they had in almost four years of walking with the Master. Their thinking still held many errors, and the message they preached had drifted somewhat from the one he had entrusted to them. But even that drift could not keep them from growing. On this night no one knew any of that yet. On this night all they knew was that they were no longer hiding.
ch25.b078: The Master had gone. That morning on the mountain he had vanished before their eyes. Yet tonight Andrew did not feel that the Master had gone. He was in his brother’s voice, and in the cold water of Siloam, and in the words Andrew himself had spoken aloud today for the first time. God was no longer a teaching they knew with their minds. He had become a living presence in their souls.
ch25.b079: Peter went up the stair first. Andrew followed, watching his back. The weight of the hand that had rested on his head in the winter grass of the highland had come down again tonight upon his shoulder. This time the hand did not lift.
ch25.b081: The events follow Paper 193, sections 3, 5 and 6, and Paper 194: the apostles kneeling unbidden in a circle on the slope of Olivet on the morning of May 18, Jesus’ farewell, and his disappearance at about a quarter to eight (193:5.1–5); the words in the upper chamber that Judas left because his love grew cold and he would not trust his brethren, and that they must trust and confide in one another (193:3.2); the one hundred and twenty gathered at Mary Mark’s house by half past ten, among them the mother of Jesus and his brother James, Peter’s report, the casting of lots downstairs between Matthias and Justus, the induction of Matthias as apostle and treasurer, and the prayer at noon (193:6.1–3, 6.6); the strange presence at about one o’clock with its joy, security and confidence, the urge to go out and proclaim, and Peter’s declaration and proposal (194:0.1–2); the spirit coming quietly, without any form, upon people at silent prayer, men and women and the family of Jesus alike (194:3.6, 3.10, 3.14–15); the forty days of hiding and the Pentecost pilgrims, Peter’s sermon at about two o’clock where the Master had last taught in the temple, the six apostles, more than an hour and a half of speaking in Greek, Hebrew and Aramaic, the Jewish leaders astounded but afraid to act, and the baptism of more than two thousand at the pool of Siloam by Peter, Andrew, James and John, ending after dark (194:1.1–5); the substance of the sermon (194:4.4); and the risen Master himself being preached in place of the gospel message (194:0.3, 2.8). Peter’s natural leadership as chief preacher (192:0.2) and John as Peter’s right hand at Pentecost (139:4.11) are also from the text.
ch25.b082: The brothers’ words that evening are developed from 139:1.6. Also drawn from the text: Andrew’s not minding being called “Simon Peter’s brother” (139:1.7), his reluctance to praise (139:1.10), his early, unspoken knowledge of the trouble in Judas (139:1.8); Peter led back to the nets through Andrew’s understanding (139:2.10, 184:2.9); Peter’s shrinking before ridicule (139:2.6); the charcoal fire and the denials in the courtyard of Annas (184:2.2–8); the garden appearance, Andrew’s warning, and Peter’s fear that he too was a betrayer (191:1.1–5); Judas never bringing a personal problem to the Master (193:4.10); forgiving seventy times and seven (139:2.5); the saying on the highland about power (140:1.6) and Peter’s pledge on the ordination night (140:6.10); the three questions on the shore and the words to Andrew (192:2.2–4, 2.7); Matthew’s hidden giving (139:7.8–9).
ch25.b083: Added as fiction: the inner thoughts of Peter and Andrew and the way their memories are woven together; weather, light, sounds and smells; the spoken suggestion to cast lots (the text says only that the apostles agreed, so the speaker is left as “someone”); the purse changing hands; the brothers’ brief exchange on the way to the temple; the officials in the shade of the columns; Matthew minding the clothes at the pool; John and James on the steps of Siloam; their leaving first so that the two brothers are alone; and the laughter in the upper chamber. The brothers’ dialogue builds a scene around the two sayings the text records, with a few short lines added before and after. Because the text does not say where the other five apostles were during the sermon, Andrew is simply shown failing to notice.
ch25.b084: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
